questions.answer: The common symptoms of diabetes include increased urination [1], feeling very thirsty [1], feeling very hungry [1], blurred vision [1], fatigue [1], sores that do not heal [1], frequent infections such as yeast infections [1]. For type 2 diabetes, additional symptoms may include pain in the feet or hands [2], sexual problems [2], chest pain [2], and vision loss [2]. Type 1 diabetes can also cause unexplained weight loss [3] and rapid onset of symptoms like needing to urinate more often, eating more but losing weight, and feeling very thirsty [4].

[1], [2] The warning signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in type 1 diabetes include: feeling very tired, having trouble breathing, having fruity-smelling breath, fainting from dehydration, and having pain in your abdomen, nausea, or vomiting. [2] Additionally, symptoms may include high levels of ketones in the urine, which can be checked by a health care team if you have DKA symptoms.

The risk factors for type 2 diabetes include being overweight or obese [2], age 35 or older [2], having a family history of diabetes [2], being African American, American Indian, Asian American, Hispanic/Latino, or Pacific Islander [2], not physically active due to physical limitations, sedentary lifestyle, or job requirements [2], having prediabetes [2], and having a history of gestational diabetes or giving birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more [2]. Additionally, waist circumference is another risk factor for type 2 diabetes [5]. [1] mentions low birth weight in children as a risk factor.
[1] shows that losing 5 to 7 percent of your starting weight can help prevent or delay type 2 diabetes, which is about 10 to 14 pounds for a 200-pound person [1].

If you have prediabetes, you can lower your chance of developing type 2 diabetes by losing weight if needed, becoming more physically active, and following a reduced-calorie eating plan [1, 2]. You should also get tested for diabetes 6 to 12 weeks after your baby is born if you had gestational diabetes during pregnancy [5].
The A1C test measures your average blood glucose level over the last 3 months [1].

[1] recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week for people with diabetes.

Waist circumference is important for diabetes risk because it is an indirect measurement of abdominal fat, which is a risk factor for both diabetes and heart disease, even in individuals with normal BMI [1].

Type 1 diabetes develops when the body's immune system destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin [1]. This destruction of beta cells leads to insufficient insulin production, which is necessary for blood glucose to enter the body’s cells and provide energy. Without enough insulin, glucose accumulates in the bloodstream, causing high blood sugar levels and potentially leading to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) if left untreated [3] or type 2 diabetes symptoms developing slowly over time [5]. The exact causes of this immune system attack are not fully understood but may involve genetic factors and environmental triggers [1, 2].

Type 2 diabetes develops when your pancreas doesn’t produce enough insulin, and your body has trouble using insulin [1]. This condition called insulin resistance occurs when the cells in your muscles, fat, and liver don't respond well to insulin [1]. Insulin resistance is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes [1], as are being overweight or obese, having a large waist size, age over 35, family history of type 2 diabetes, certain ethnicities, lack of physical activity, smoking, having prediabetes, and having had gestational diabetes before [1-2]. Insulin resistance can also be caused by genetic factors [4].

Some medicines can raise the risk of diabetes [1]. Insulin injections and other medications like metformin, sulfonylureas, and sodium-glucose co-transporters type 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors are used to manage blood sugar levels in people with diabetes [3] [4]. Additionally, statins may slightly increase the chance of developing diabetes [1], though their benefits for heart disease outweigh this risk.

The risk factors for high blood pressure include unhealthy lifestyle habits like poor diet, excessive alcohol consumption, lack of physical activity, and insufficient sleep [1, 4]. Other factors that cannot be changed are age, family history, genetics, race/ethnicity, and sex. Social and economic factors such as income level, education, job type, and stress at work can also increase risk [2]. Age is a factor; blood pressure tends to rise with age due to natural changes in the body [3]. Certain medical conditions like kidney disease, thyroid problems, sleep apnea, and metabolic syndrome are linked to high blood pressure [4]. Lastly, experiencing discrimination and poverty has been associated with an increased risk of developing high blood pressure [2].

Eating more vegetables and fruits [1], sitting less [1], being physically active [1], losing weight if overweight or obese [1], taking medicines as prescribed by your health care professional [1] are lifestyle changes that help lower high blood pressure [1]. Additionally, avoiding alcohol, getting regular physical activity, aiming for a healthy weight, quitting smoking, controlling cholesterol and blood sugar levels, managing stress, and ensuring enough good-quality sleep also contribute to lowering high blood pressure [5, 4, 5].

Unhealthy eating patterns, including consuming a lot of saturated fats and refined carbohydrates (such as white bread, pasta, and white rice), can lead to overweight and obesity, high blood cholesterol, atherosclerosis, and plaque buildup in the heart's arteries [1]. Drinking too much alcohol can raise your blood pressure and your risk for heart disease. Drinking more than two drinks a day for men or one drink a day for women can raise your levels of cholesterol and triglycerides [2]. Stress can cause your arteries to tighten, indirectly raising your risk if it makes you more likely to smoke or overeat foods that are high in fat and added sugars [1].
